### Summary

pyharp's tests are of two kinds: C++ programs built with GoogleTest and run by `ctest`, and Python files run by
`pytest`. A reader who wants to know what is verified needs three lists: the tests that exist in the tree, the tests
the build registers, and the tests the continuous-integration job runs. This section gives the three lists at the
pin, the result of running every test that exists, and what that shows about coverage.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** What pyharp's test files check, and which of them CI runs (Tests layer).

**Data.** 22 C++ test files, 7 Python files in `tests/`, 15 in `tests/spectra/`.

**Placement.** `ctest` after a CMake build with `BUILD_TESTS=ON`; `pytest` from the source root.

**Activation.** CMake option `BUILD_TESTS` (default on); CI on every push to `main` and every change proposed against it.

**Guarantee / limits.** CI runs 14 C++ test programs and 3 Python files; the other 27 files are not run.

**Evidence.** The Tests layer of @sec-ch10-test-suite.
:::

Local symbols: none.

The C++ tests are registered one by one with the CMake macro `setup_test`; a file that is not named there is
neither built nor run. The Python test files are copied into the build tree but never registered with `ctest`.
The CI job builds the tests, runs `ctest`, and runs three files of `tests/spectra/` with `pytest`.

### Derivation

None: this section states facts about the test harness and has no equations.

### Numerical method

The method here is the harness itself. `setup_test` builds `tests/<name>.cpp` into an executable
`<name>.<build type>` linked against the pyharp library and `gtest_main`, and registers it with `add_test`
(`setup_test`, {{< code cmake/macros/macro_setup_test.cmake repo=pyharp >}}). `tests/CMakeLists.txt`
({{< code tests/CMakeLists.txt repo=pyharp >}}) calls it for 14 files; it copies every `tests/*.py` into the build
tree with `configure_file`, but its `add_test(... pytest ...)` line is commented out. The workflow
({{< code .github/workflows/ci.yml repo=pyharp >}}) has one test job, `build-and-test`, on `ubuntu-latest` and
`macOS-latest` with Python 3.11, torch 2.10.0 (the CPU wheel on Linux) and `pydisort==1.7.1` installed with
`--no-deps`; it configures with `-DNETCDF=ON -DBUILD_TESTS=ON`, runs `ctest --output-on-failure`, and runs
`pytest` on `tests/spectra/test_hitemp_lines.py`, `test_line_kernel.py` and `test_hitran_lines.py`. No job builds
with CUDA.

Many of the C++ tests are parametrised over device and precision by the fixture `DeviceTest`
({{< code tests/device_testing.hpp DeviceTest repo=pyharp >}}): CPU float32, CPU float64, CUDA float32 and CUDA
float64. `DeviceTest::SetUp` ({{< code tests/device_testing.hpp DeviceTest::SetUp repo=pyharp >}}) skips the CUDA
cases when `torch::cuda::is_available()` is false. The skip tests the torch installation, not whether pyharp was
built with CUDA, so a CPU-only pyharp linked against a CUDA-enabled torch on a machine with a GPU runs the CUDA
cases and fails them (Tests layer below).

The inventory: 22 C++ test files, of which `ctest` registers 14; 3 of the 22 contain no assertion macro
(`test_composition.cpp`, `test_hypsometric.cpp`, `test_yaml_input.cpp`), and `test_bbflux.cpp` asserts only
output shapes. None of the 7 files in `tests/` and 3 of the 15 in `tests/spectra/` are run by CI[^ch10-inv].

### Limits

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
A green CI run covers the 14 registered C++ programs and 3 spectra files only; the Python tests of the solvers,
including `tests/test_toon.py`, are not run.
:::

- **CI coverage (CANDIDATE, test registration).** 27 of the 44 test files are not run by CI: 8 C++ files are not

- **Device gate (CANDIDATE, test fixture).** The CUDA cases run whenever torch reports a GPU, whether or not pyharp

### Summary

pyharp compiles against the C++ headers and shared library of an installed pydisort, and at run time loads
whichever pydisort is installed. This section states which versions the package accepts, which one CI tests, and
what happens when the version pyharp was built against differs from the one it runs with.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** The pydisort versions pyharp builds and runs against, and the result of mixing them.

**Data.** `pydisort>=1.7.1` (build and run requirement); CI installs 1.7.1.

**Placement.** Build time (CMake finds pydisort) and import time (the extension loads its library).

**Activation.** Always; no option.

**Guarantee / limits.** Matched builds pass; built against 1.7.1 and run with 1.8.13 aborts (Limits layer).

**Evidence.** The Tests layer of @sec-ch10-packaging.
:::

Local symbols: none.

The requirement has a lower bound and no upper bound, so `pip install pyharp` installs the newest pydisort, 1.8.13 when
the checks ran[^ch10-pkg-header], while CI builds and tests against 1.7.1 only.

### Derivation

None: this section states facts about packaging and has no equations.

### Numerical method

At build time `FindDisort.cmake` asks the Python interpreter for the installed `pydisort` package and uses its
headers and `libdisort_release.so` (`__disort_determine_version`,
{{< code cmake/modules/FindDisort.cmake repo=pyharp >}}). The extension built by
`setup.py` (`ext_module`, {{< code setup.py ext_module repo=pyharp >}}) records the run-time search path
`$ORIGIN/../pydisort/lib`, so at import it loads the library of whatever pydisort is installed then. Both
`pyproject.toml` lists, `[build-system] requires` and `[project] dependencies`, say `pydisort>=1.7.1`
({{< code pyproject.toml repo=pyharp >}}); the CI job installs `pydisort==1.7.1` with `--no-deps`
({{< code .github/workflows/ci.yml repo=pyharp >}}).

pyharp's DISORT band solver holds a `DisortImpl` object, a C++ class that pydisort declares in its header
(`DisortImpl`, {{< code src/disort.hpp DisortImpl repo=pydisort >}}). pyharp's compiled code fixes the size and
member layout of that class from the header it was built with, and pydisort's library code uses the layout of its
own header. The two agree only when the versions agree. In the 1.8.13 wheel the header declares one more data
member in `DisortImpl` than at the pin, a `torch::Tensor cuda_workspace_` described as reused CUDA scratch
storage[^ch10-pkg-header].

### Summary

pyharp's options are C++ structs; pybind11 code in `python/csrc` exposes them to Python, and hand-written stub
files (`python/*.pyi`) describe them to editors and type checkers. Nothing generates the bindings or the stubs from
the structs, so the three can drift apart. This section compares them option by option at the pin.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** Which C++ options a Python user can set, and which the stubs declare.

**Data.** 9 option structs, 58 options and flag accessors; the installed `pyharp` module; `python/*.pyi`.

**Placement.** Import of `pyharp` (bindings); static analysis (stubs).

**Activation.** Always.

**Guarantee / limits.** 16 options have no binding and 29 no stub (Tests layer); none is checked by CI.

**Evidence.** The Tests layer of @sec-ch10-bindings.
:::

Local symbols: none.

An option missing from the bindings can be set only through YAML or C++; one missing from the stubs works but is
invisible to type checkers and editor completion.

### Derivation

None: this section compares interfaces and has no equations.

### Numerical method

Each option of a struct is declared with the macro `ADD_ARG(type, name)`, which generates a getter and a setter of
that name; some solver structs add boolean accessors that test a comma-separated `flags` string
(`ToonMcKay89OptionsImpl`, {{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89.hpp ToonMcKay89OptionsImpl repo=pyharp >}}). The
bindings expose an option by naming it once more with the macro `ADD_OPTION` of `python/csrc/pyoptions.hpp`, for
example in `bind_rtsolver` ({{< code python/csrc/pyrtsolver.cpp bind_rtsolver repo=pyharp >}}); the stubs declare
it again as a `def` in `python/pyharp.pyi` ({{< code python/pyharp.pyi repo=pyharp >}}). The check
`bindings_diff.py` reads every `ADD_ARG` and flag accessor under `src/`, looks each up as an attribute of the
installed Python class, and as a `def` under the class of the same name in the stubs.

### Summary

A comparison test asks whether a solver agrees with a reference on the cases someone chose. A floor, a clamp or a
dropped term can pass every such test and still break a law the answer must obey on every input: a layer that
only scatters must absorb nothing, an isothermal column must carry no net flux, a flux cannot be negative, and a
column with no opacity must pass the boundary fluxes through unchanged. This section runs those laws as checks on
the full band path of both solvers, lists every floor and clamp in the compiled code with a measurement of what it
changes, and shows that each check goes red when the term or floor it guards is removed.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** Invariants of the band fluxes: @eq-ch10-invariants-closure to @eq-ch10-invariants-zero.

**Data.** Band fluxes $F^{\pm}$ [$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$] at 21 levels; 46 band runs; 91 guards of the source.

**Placement.** `RadiationBandImpl::forward` and the Toon and DISORT solvers it calls.

**Activation.** Always (checks of the report, run by hand against a build of the pin).

**Guarantee / limits.** All 18 checks pass at the pin; five candidate defects are reproduced.

**Evidence.** The Tests layer of @sec-ch10-invariants.
:::

Local symbols: $S$, the flux scale of a band (the incident beam $\mu_0F_0$ of a shortwave band, $\pi\bar B$ of the
surface temperature for a longwave band) [$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$]; $a_k$, the energy absorbed by layer $k$
[$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$]; $Q^{z}_k$, $Q^{p}_k$, the heating rate of layer $k$ per unit volume and per unit mass
[$\mathrm{K\,s^{-1}}$]; $x_k$, the thickness of layer $k$ in $\ln p$ [-]; $\bar p_k$, the pressure of layer $k$
[Pa]. $\bar B(T)$ is the band Planck integral of @sec-ch04-planck.

Every check reports a dimensionless residual $\epsilon$ against a tolerance whose reason is stated where it is used.
Four checks measure the thresholds of the kernels from their inputs (`[T1]` to `[T4]`); a scratch build with one
line changed at a time measures the other guards and runs the break tests.

### Derivation

Levels are numbered from the surface, $k = 0$, to the top of the atmosphere, $k = L$; layer $k$ lies between levels
$k$ and $k+1$. $F^{+}_k$ and $F^{-}_k$ are the upward and downward band fluxes at level $k$, the downward one
including the direct beam, and $F_{\mathrm{net},k} = F^{+}_k - F^{-}_k$ is positive upward. The energy layer $k$
absorbs is what enters it less what leaves it:

$$
a_k = \left(F^{-}_{k+1} - F^{+}_{k+1}\right) + \left(F^{+}_k - F^{-}_k\right) = F_{\mathrm{net},k} -
F_{\mathrm{net},k+1}.
$$ {#eq-ch10-invariants-absorbed}

<!-- equation-check: eq-ch10-invariants-absorbed invariants.py [E2] -->
`RadiationImpl::forward` returns $F_{\mathrm{net}}$ at every level
({{< code src/radiation/radiation.cpp RadiationImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}), so $a_k$ is a difference of two of
its outputs. Summed over the column, the interior levels cancel:

$$
\sum_{k=0}^{L-1} a_k = F_{\mathrm{net},0} - F_{\mathrm{net},L}.
$$ {#eq-ch10-invariants-closure}

<!-- equation-check: eq-ch10-invariants-closure invariants.py [E1] -->
The sum is an identity of the solver's own output. It becomes a check when the two ends are replaced by what the
boundary conditions prescribe rather than what the solver returned. At the top the downward flux is the incident
one, $F^{-}_L = \mu_0F_0$ for a shortwave band and $0$ or $\pi\bar B(T_L)$ for a longwave band (no or full top
emission). At a Lambertian surface of albedo $A_s$ the upward flux is $F^{+}_0 = A_sF^{-}_0$ in the shortwave and
$F^{+}_0 = (1 - A_s)\pi\bar B(T_0) + A_sF^{-}_0$ in the longwave with `hard_surface`, with the band Planck integral
$\bar B$ of the band's own solver. The closure residual is then

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{E}} = \frac{1}{S}\left|\sum_k a_k - \left[\left(F^{+}_0 - F^{-}_0\right)_{\mathrm{bc}} -
\left(F^{+}_L - F^{-}_L\right)_{\mathrm{bc}}\right]\right|,
$$ {#eq-ch10-invariants-residual}

<!-- equation-check: eq-ch10-invariants-residual invariants.py [E1] -->
where the subscript bc marks a flux replaced by its boundary value. By @eq-ch10-invariants-closure,
$\epsilon_{\mathrm{E}}$ is the sum of the two boundary residuals: it is zero exactly when the solver meets both
boundary rows of its system and the band sums its quadrature points consistently, and it is the energy the column
gains or loses otherwise. The Toon shortwave bottom row, for example, is the surface reflection of the diffuse and
the direct flux (`bsurf`, {{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_shortwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_shortwave repo=pyharp >}}).

Three special cases fix the answer layer by layer, not only in sum. With $\omega = 1$ and no emission no layer
absorbs, $a_k = 0$ for every $k$ (@eq-ch02-conservation-divergence). The band clamps $\omega$ to $1 - 10^{-12}$
(@sec-ch02-conservation), so a layer absorbs at most $(1 - \omega)\Delta\tau_n \cdot 4\pi J$, with $J$ the mean
intensity. In the thickest test column ($\tau = 40$) the two-stream estimate $4\pi J \approx 2(F^{+} + F^{-})$ plus
the beam term $S/\mu_0$ stays below $5S$ (`[E2]`), so the clamp allows at most
$10^{-12} \cdot 40 \cdot 5S = 2\times10^{-10}S$; the tolerance $10^{-9}$ covers that and the round-off. In an
isothermal column at temperature $T$ with full top emission and a black surface, every intensity equals $\bar B(T)$,
so $F^{\pm}_k = \pi\bar B(T)$ and $F_{\mathrm{net},k} = 0$ at every level. In a shortwave band no so $a_k \ge 0$; in a
longwave band with a hard surface and no top illumination the intensities are averages of Planck functions of the
column's temperatures, so $F^{\pm}_k \le \pi\bar B(T_{\max})$.

The heating rate of layer $k$ follows from $a_k$ in two ways. Let $p_k$ be the pressure of level $k$,
$x_k = \ln(p_k/p_{k+1})$ the thickness of layer $k$ in $\ln p$, $\Delta p_k = p_k - p_{k+1}$, and
$\bar p_k = (p_kp_{k+1})^{1/2}$ the layer pressure (the geometric mean of its levels, which `calc_dz_hypsometric`
assumes when it rebuilds the levels from layer values). Per unit volume, with pyharp's hypsometric thickness
$\Delta z_k = (RT_k/|g_1|)x_k$ and the layer density $\rho_k = \bar p_k/(RT_k)$, the heating rate is
$Q^{z}_k = a_k/(\rho_kc_p\Delta z_k)$; per unit mass of the pressure grid it is $Q^{p}_k = |g_1|a_k/(c_p\Delta p_k)$.
Here $|g_1|$ is the magnitude of gravity, $R$ the specific gas constant and $c_p$ the heat capacity at constant
pressure. With $p_k = \bar p_ke^{x_k/2}$ and $p_{k+1} = \bar p_ke^{-x_k/2}$ their ratio does not depend on the
fluxes:

$$
\frac{Q^{z}_k}{Q^{p}_k} = \frac{\Delta p_k}{|g_1|\rho_k\Delta z_k} = \frac{\Delta p_k}{\bar p_kx_k}
= \frac{e^{x_k/2} - e^{-x_k/2}}{x_k} = \frac{2\sinh(x_k/2)}{x_k}.
$$ {#eq-ch10-invariants-heating}

<!-- equation-check: eq-ch10-invariants-heating invariants.py [E4] -->
The check compares the ratio formed with `calc_dz_hypsometric`
({{< code src/radiation/calc_dz_hypsometric.cpp calc_dz_hypsometric repo=pyharp >}}) against the right-hand side;
their difference is round-off.

A column with no opacity, $\Delta\tau_n = 0$ in every layer, attenuates nothing and emits nothing:

$$
F^{-}_k = F^{-}_L, \qquad F^{+}_k = F^{+}_0, \qquad a_k = 0 \quad \text{for every } k,
$$ {#eq-ch10-invariants-zero}

<!-- equation-check: eq-ch10-invariants-zero invariants.py [Z1] -->
With no extinction the band's weighted albedo and moments are $0/0$; `divide_where_positive` in
`RadiationBandImpl::forward` ({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}})
returns 0 there. For a small optical depth the fluxes move by $O(\tau)$: $\mu_0|F(\tau) - F(0)|/(\tau S)$ is the
derivative of the flux in $\tau$, of order 1 for both the beam and diffuse light. A jump or a cancellation in a floor
shows up as a slope many orders larger; the bound $100$ leaves room for any physical slope of these columns. What is
exact: @eq-ch10-invariants-absorbed to @eq-ch10-invariants-zero. What is truncated: nothing; the checks hold the
solvers to their own equations, not to a reference solution. The executable checks are
`derivation-checks/ch10/invariants.py`, `opacity_probe.py` and `model_probe/model_probe.cpp`.

### Numerical method

Every case runs the path a user's YAML runs. A TorchScript opacity (`type: jit`) returns, for each of three quadrature
points of the band (weights 0.2, 0.5, 0.3), the extinction, single-scattering albedo $\omega$ and the
Henyey-Greenstein moments $g^l$ that the case prescribes. `RadiationBandImpl::forward` multiplies the extinction by
the layer thickness, weights and divides the albedo and moments (`divide_where_positive`), clamps $\omega$ and calls
the solver; `RadiationImpl::forward` sums the band over its weights and returns the net flux, the surface downward and
the top upward flux. The column has 20 layers on a grid uniform in $\ln p$ from $10^5$ to $10^3$ Pa; each layer
carries the share of the column optical depth that its pressure thickness has, so the bottom layer holds 21 per cent
of it. Five bands are solved: Toon shortwave, DISORT shortwave (4 streams, `nphase` set to 0, see `[D1]` in the Tests
layer), Toon longwave with `hard_surface`, Toon longwave without it and DISORT longwave (500 to 600
$\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, level temperatures 300 K at the surface to 200 K at the top). The shortwave cases are a nominal
column ($\tau$ = 0.5, 2, 8; $\omega$ = 0.3, 0.8, 0.95; $g = 0.6$; $A_s = 0.3$; $\mu_0 = 0.6$) and its edge cases:
$\omega = 0$ with $A_s = 0$ (the beam-only formula of the Toon kernel) and with $A_s = 0.3$, $\omega = 1$,
$\omega = 1 - 10^{-6}$ with $A_s = 0.99$, $A_s = 0$, $A_s = 1$, grazing beams $\mu_0 = 0.02$ and $10^{-3}$, a thick
column ($\tau$ up to 400) and $\tau = 0$. The longwave cases vary $\omega$ (0, 0.3, 0.99), $A_s$ (0, 0.1, 0.99) and
$\tau$ (0 to 400) the same way.

Two further kinds of check do not solve a band. `opacity_probe.py` runs the condensate opacities that need no data
file (`water-ice-fu96-98`, `water-liquid-mie`, `water-cloud-temperature-switch`) on layers with zero and with
positive concentration, and the table interpolation `interpn` on a table with a zero entry stored as each table
opacity's floor. `model_probe.cpp` steps `RadiationModelImpl::forward`, which has no Python binding, once with a
Toon shortwave band and compares the energy it adds to the atmosphere and surface with the energy that enters at
the top.

`floor_inventory.py` scans every line the build compiles (`src/` and the five subdirectories `src/CMakeLists.txt`
globs) and the Python package for the guard patterns (`clamp`, `fmin`/`fmax`, `std::min`/`max`, `epsilon`, a small
literal, `torch::where`, a comparison with zero), outside comments. Each hit must match one entry of its table,
which names the kind (floor, clamp, switch, division guard, refusal, or not a floor) and the check that measures
it; a hit that matches none fails the check.

`break_tests.py` clones the pinned tree into a scratch directory, builds `libharp`, and runs the three checks
against a copy of the installed package that loads the scratch library. One mutation at a time, it changes one line

1. `RadiationBandImpl::forward` ({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}})
   divides the weighted albedo and moments with `divide_where_positive`, which returns 0 where the weight is 0,
   clamps $\omega$ to $1 - 10^{-12}$ in double precision ($1 - 10^{-6}$ in single), and refuses a negative level
   temperature.
2. `toon_mckay89_shortwave` ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_shortwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_shortwave repo=pyharp >}})
   takes the beam-only formula when every layer has $\omega \le 10^{-12}$ and $A_s \le 10^{-12}$, replaces
   $\gamma_2 = 0$ by $10^{-10}$, moves $\mu_0$ off the resonance $\lambda\mu_0 = 1$ by the square root of the
   machine precision, caps the layer exponential at $e^{35}$, zeroes $|x_{k2}|$ below $10^{-30}$ of its partner and
   floors the midpoint beam product at 0 (@sec-ch04-shortwave).
3. `toon_mckay89_longwave` ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_longwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_longwave repo=pyharp >}})
   takes the Planck function constant across a layer with $\Delta\tau_n \le 10^{-6}$, drops the scattering source of
   its intensity sweep for $\omega \le 10^{-4}$, caps its exponentials at $e^{35}$ and uses the limit 1 of
   $(e^x - 1)/x$ at $x = 0$ (`longwave_exprel`) (@sec-ch04-longwave).
4. `dtridgl` ({{< code src/rtsolver/dtridgl_impl.h dtridgl repo=pyharp >}}) replaces a zero pivot by $10^{-12}$.
5. `RadiationModelImpl::forward` ({{< code src/integrator/radiation_model.cpp RadiationModelImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}})
   forces the surface with the downward surface flux less $\sigma T_s^4$ and clamps the atmospheric and surface
   temperatures to $[20, 1000]$ K after every step.

- `[T2]` The Toon longwave switch at $\omega = 10^{-4}$ is a jump of $8.2\times10^{-6}$ of $S$ for a change of

  $L \cdot$ `nphase` phase values whenever `nphase` $\ge 1$ and `old_intensity_correction` is off, so the value left
  in memory decides whether a band allocates a phase table it never uses or aborts when the product overflows; the
  break tests aborted this way until the bands of `invariants.py` set `nphase` to 0.

### Limits

- **Gas-giant lower boundary (CANDIDATE, Toon longwave).** Unbounded upward flux for an optically thin bottom layer
  without `hard_surface` (`[Z3]` above); the checks `[E1]` and `[Z2]` therefore cover the hard-surface band only.
- **Scattering switch at $\omega = 10^{-4}$ (CANDIDATE, Toon longwave).** A jump of $8.2\times10^{-6}$ of $S$
  (`[T2]`).
- **`RadiationModel` surface budget and temperature clamp (CANDIDATE).** `[M1]`, `[M2]` above; `RadiationModel` has no
  Python binding and no test of its own at the pin.
- **DISORT internals.** The checks run pydisort as a wheel; no break test mutates cdisort, so `[P3]` has no break
  test, and of cdisort's guard lines only the five on the exercised paths are listed (`[F4]`). The newer intensity
  correction, whose intensities are not finite from pydisort, is the subject of @sec-ch03-intcorr and is not run.
- **Unwritten `nphase` (CANDIDATE, DISORT band).** `[D1]` above; the DISORT bands of these checks set it to 0.
- **Opacity tables.** The table floors are measured through `interpn` on a two-node table (`[Z5]`), not through the
  table opacities themselves, which need data files these checks do not ship. The offline line-by-line tools of
  `python/spectra/` are listed but not measured.
- **Device and precision.** All runs are on CPU in double precision; the single-precision albedo margin $10^{-6}$
  and the CUDA kernels are not exercised.
